::: {.callout-warning appearance="default"}
**This is the highest-yield page on the site, but only if you use it correctly.** The five mock prompts below are written at the difficulty level Hammad will set on the cumulative final. Each one demands integration of frames + dates + counterargument across at least two of the three throughlines. **Do not skim the sample answers.** Outline first; only then read the model.
:::

## How to use this page

The temptation, on a study site like this one, is to read the sample answer first and reason backward to the prompt. That is the worst possible use of your time. The exam will reward whether *you* can build a structure under time pressure — not whether you can recognize one when it is shown to you. So the protocol is:

1. **Read the prompt and decoder.** Underline the verb (compare, defend, analyze, contest) and the named actors/frames.
2. **Spend 5 minutes outlining.** Thesis + 3 topic sentences + tie-back. On paper. Closed eyes if you have to.
3. **Only then read the model outline** and compare. If your structure differs, ask yourself which is more defensible — not which is closer to the model.
4. **Read the sample answer last.** Mark which dates and citations you would not have produced cold. Add those to your cram-sheet drill list.
5. **Re-read the rubric for that prompt.** The rubric is the actual grading function — internalize it, not the prose.

Five prompts, ~6,000 words of A-grade sample prose, plus rubrics. If you do this once for each prompt — outline cold, then compare — you have effectively rehearsed the exam five times under live conditions. That is the highest-leverage prep available to you in the final week.

## Universal rubric — what Hammad rewards on every essay

::: {.callout-tip}
**The four invariants.** Across all 17 study-guide questions, Hammad consistently rewards: (1) **structure** — explicit thesis in the first paragraph, three evidentiary moves, tie-back; (2) **citation density** — author + year inline at least four times, with the *correct* author for the frame; (3) **throughline tie-back** — the final sentence should connect your specific argument to one of the three master throughlines (API→Accords pivot, Nash carousel, Iran's linkage engine); (4) **counterargument with rebuttal** — at least one explicit "one might object that…" move, defeated on the merits rather than waved away. Reactive prose without these four loses an entire letter grade even when the facts are right.
:::

# Prompt 1 — The Pivot

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Prompt.** Compare the regional logics of the 2002 Arab Peace Initiative and the 2020 Abraham Accords. To what extent does the post-October-7 Saudi-Israeli normalization track represent a reversion to API logic, a continuation of Accords logic, or a new equilibrium? Use at least two of Hammad's lecture frames in your analysis.
:::

## Decoder

The verb is **compare** plus a three-way **classify**: API logic, Accords logic, or new equilibrium. Hammad is not asking for a chronology; he is asking which sequencing rule governs the Saudi track in 2026. The "regional logic" phrase is doing work — it forces you to abstract above the documents and identify the *sequencing rule* each embodies. API: Palestinian state first, normalization second. Accords: normalization first, Palestinian file deferred to a vague "regional architecture" play. The Saudi post-October-7 position is closer to API in sequencing but lacks the API's text and its multilateral Arab League imprimatur — that is the analytical sweet spot.

The throughline this maps to is the **API → Abraham Accords pivot**, with a partial reversion as the working hypothesis. Frames most useful: Gause (primacy ≠ hegemony, why the convergence happened), and the regime-public delinking literature (Lynch on the wager that publics no longer constrain regimes — falsified by Arab Barometer 2024). Bellin can also enter through the side door: the regimes that signed the Accords could absorb the public-opinion cost because their coercive apparatuses were robust enough to delink.

**Common student misreading:** treating the Accords as a "failure" because Saudi did not sign. They were a structural shift in sequencing, durably so, even though Riyadh declined to ratify the new equilibrium. A second misreading: claiming October 7 "killed" the Accords. None of the four signatories withdrew.

## Outline

- **Thesis (intro).** API and Accords are competing sequencing rules — Palestinian-state-first vs. normalization-first — and the post-October-7 Saudi position is a partial API reversion in *sequencing* without restoring API's *text*, producing a new hybrid equilibrium rather than a clean return to either.
- **Body 1.** API as sequencing rule: 28 March 2002 Beirut, full Arab normalization conditioned on 1967 lines plus Palestinian state plus refugee resolution; functioned as a normative anchor even without execution.
- **Body 2.** Accords as inversion: 13 August / 11 September / 23 October / 10 December 2020, four bilateral deals priced by US side payments (F-35s, Western Sahara, SST de-listing), Palestinian file demoted to footnote — Lynch's regime-public delinking wager.
- **Body 3.** Post-October-7 Saudi track: Riyadh suspends but does not cancel; MBS in September 2024 re-attaches normalization to "independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem capital"; September 2025 Saudi-French two-state initiative at UNGA. Sequencing has reverted; text has not.
- **Conclusion + tie-back.** New equilibrium, not reversion: API's sequencing logic has reasserted itself because publics constrained regimes more than Lynch's critics expected, but the API's multilateral Arab League frame is gone — what remains is bilateral conditionality. The pivot was real; its reversal is partial.

## Sample answer

> The 2002 Arab Peace Initiative and the 2020 Abraham Accords are best read not as two diplomatic documents but as two competing **sequencing rules** for Arab–Israeli relations — the *prize* model and the *vehicle* model — and the post-October-7 Saudi track is a partial reversion to the first without restoration of the second. Adopting Hammad's framing, the API → Accords pivot was the most consequential normative shift in regional diplomacy since Camp David 1978; what we are watching since October 2023 is not a clean return to API but the formation of a new hybrid equilibrium in which API's *sequencing* has reasserted itself even as its multilateral Arab League architecture has not. Two of Hammad's frames anchor this argument: Gause (2024) on why convergence around the Iranian threat made the pivot possible at all, and the regime-public delinking debate (Lynch 2024) on why the wager that Arab publics no longer constrained regimes was falsified after October 7. The thesis: API logic is back as a sequencing rule; Accords logic survives as an institutional residue; what we have now is neither pure form.
>
> [::: {.thesis}
> The 2002 API and 2020 Accords are sequencing rules, not just deals — and the Saudi-Israeli track in 2026 has restored API's sequencing without restoring its text, producing a hybrid equilibrium rather than a true reversion.
> :::]{.thesis}
>
> The API, adopted unanimously at the Beirut Arab League Summit on 28 March 2002, formalized the *prize* model. Twenty-two Arab League states (and through OIC re-endorsement, fifty-seven Muslim-majority states) committed to full normalization with Israel in exchange for three Israeli concessions: full withdrawal from territories occupied in June 1967, an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as capital, and a just resolution of the refugee question per UNGA 194. The Sharon government dismissed it; no negotiation followed. Yet the API became the regional template precisely because no Arab regime could publicly abandon it without facing domestic legitimacy costs. As Khalidi (2020) argues in his settler-colonial framing, the API encoded a normative claim that Arab states had collectively offered the maximum compatible with sovereignty — and Israel had refused. Whether one accepts Khalidi's normative valence or not, the structural point is uncontested: from 2002 through 2020, the sequencing rule was Palestinian state first, normalization second, and every Arab regime cited it when cornered.
>
> The Accords inverted that rule. The four bilateral instruments — UAE on 13 August 2020 (formalized 15 September), Bahrain on 11 September, Sudan on 23 October, Morocco on 10 December — replaced the API's *prize* logic with a *vehicle* logic: normalize first, and use the resulting regional architecture to eventually pull Israel toward Palestinian accommodation. The Trump brokerage made this possible through side payments that priced normalization to Arab regimes without requiring Israeli concessions: a roughly $23 billion F-35 package for the UAE, US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, and removal of Sudan from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list. Gause's (2024) account of why the alignment crystallized in 2020 rather than earlier emphasizes convergent threat perception — Iran's post-2003 expansion through Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen, capped by the September 2019 Aramco strikes — combined with perceived US retrenchment. This is also where Bellin (2004) enters through the side door: the regimes that signed the Accords could absorb domestic backlash because their coercive apparatuses were patrimonially organized, well-financed by hydrocarbon rents, and internationally backed — exactly the three conditions Bellin specifies for authoritarian robustness. Lynch's (2024) "regime-public delinking" wager was the operative bet: that Arab publics no longer cared enough about Palestine to constrain regimes. The Accords' published declarations dispense with Palestine in a single vague clause about a "just, comprehensive resolution."
>
> One might object — as Ross and Indyk in defense of the Accords have — that the *vehicle* logic was not abandonment but a sophisticated outside-in play: build the architecture first, generate stakes, eventually pull all parties including a future Palestinian state into the system. The objection is real but does not rescue the Accords from the empirical test that arrived in 2023. Arab Barometer data through 2024 show support for normalization never exceeded 13% in any of the seven Arab Barometer countries; in Saudi Arabia, opposition rose from 38% in 2022 to 68% by early 2024 (Robbins 2024). The wager Lynch (2024) identified was falsified: publics did constrain regimes, especially after the visual saturation of Gaza in 2023–24 made any quiet normalization politically untenable. Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack — whatever its full motivational mix — demonstrably exploited this constraint. Internal Hamas documents and Sinwar communications, with caveats about provenance, suggest derailing Saudi-Israel normalization was at minimum one strategic motivation; the spoiler theory is more plausible than not.
>
> The post-October-7 Saudi track has therefore reverted to API *sequencing* without restoring API *text*. By October 2023 the Biden mega-deal — a US-Saudi defense pact, civilian nuclear cooperation including domestic enrichment, and a still-undefined Palestinian component — was within reach; Tom Friedman was openly predicting a deal by Q1 2024. After October 7, Riyadh suspended active negotiation while keeping channels open. In September 2024, MBS publicly stated on Saudi state TV that the Kingdom would not establish diplomatic relations with Israel without an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as capital — a near-verbatim API echo. Saudi Arabia then co-led the September 2025 Saudi-French two-state initiative at UNGA, producing a wave of European recognitions of Palestine. As of May 2026, the second Trump administration's claim that Riyadh had dropped the Palestinian-state precondition has been publicly denied by Saudi officials. The sequencing rule operative in Riyadh today is, in substance, the API rule.
>
> Yet this is not a clean reversion to API logic. Three differences make the current equilibrium new rather than restored. First, the API was a *multilateral* Arab League instrument; the Saudi position in 2026 is *bilateral* conditionality, not a renewed Arab League consensus offer. Second, none of the four Accords signatories withdrew — Bahrain's parliament voted to suspend ties in November 2023 but the executive declined to formalize the recall, the UAE issued public condemnations while keeping AI/defense cooperation quiet, Morocco saw air links cut but kept Western Sahara recognition intact. The institutional residue of the Accords is real (Carnegie 2025; Atlantic Council 2025 — "durable but diminished"). Third, China has entered the security-broker role through the 10 March 2023 Beijing-mediated Saudi-Iran rapprochement, altering the external constraint that any Saudi-US-Israeli deal must clear. The API was a deal between Arab regimes and Washington's mediation; the post-October-7 equilibrium is a deal among Arab regimes, Washington, *and* Beijing as a hedging guarantor.
>
> The defensible synthesis is therefore that the API → Accords pivot was a real structural shift, durably visible in the four signatures that survive Gaza, but its core sequencing rule was reversed by the events of 2023–24. Lynch's wager about the regime-public gap held for the regimes that had already signed; it broke for the regime that had not. Saudi Arabia is the regional pricing power for any wider Sunni-Israeli accommodation, and by 2026 Riyadh has restored Palestinian-state conditionality as the price tag — a partial API logic without API's multilateral text or refugee clause. The pivot was real; its reversal is partial; the equilibrium that has formed is a hybrid that cannot be classified neatly as either. That is precisely why the post-October-7 trajectory belongs at the center of any account of the regional system: it tracks the throughline most directly, showing both that sequencing rules can pivot and that they can pivot back without restoring the prior text.

## Grading rubric — what an A vs. C answer looks like

| Dimension | A-grade | C-grade |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis | Names sequencing rule as the unit of comparison; classifies post-Oct-7 as hybrid, not pure reversion | "Compares" two documents without abstracting to a sequencing rule |
| Evidence density | 6+ specific dates (3/28/02, 8/13/20, 9/15/20, 10/23/20, 12/10/20, 9/24 MBS statement, 9/25 UNGA); inline (Gause 2024), (Lynch 2024), (Bellin 2004), (Khalidi 2020), Arab Barometer numbers | Vague references to "the Accords" and "after Oct 7" without dates |
| Frame integration | At least two frames (Gause, Lynch, Bellin) deployed with the *correct attribution* and the right operative claim | Frame-name dropping without using the operative claim |
| Counterargument | Engages Ross/Indyk outside-in defense and rebuts on Arab Barometer evidence | No counterargument, or strawman version dismissed in one sentence |
| Tie-back | Final sentence connects to API → Accords pivot throughline as the master frame | Ends with a summary, not a connection to a throughline |

# Prompt 2 — The Engine

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Prompt.** Analyze Iran's role as the linkage between the Israeli-Palestinian and Gulf-security spheres. How does the December 2024 collapse of the Assad regime change the structural validity of treating Iran as the regional "engine"? Engage Goodarzi's account of the Iran-Syria alliance and at least one counterargument.
:::

## Decoder

This prompt is the throughline-3 question in undisguised form: Iran's linkage engine. The verb sequence is **analyze, then assess change**. Step one is to reconstruct the engine: how Iran connected the two spheres before December 2024 (Hezbollah as forward arm, Syria as land bridge, "unity of the arenas" doctrine). Step two is to take a position on what the Assad collapse did to that linkage — full break, partial degradation, or no change because the linkage was always rhetorical. Hammad's grading hand here will reward the **structural-versus-functional distinction**: structurally Iran remains the only actor with proxies at both ends, but functionally the doctrine has been falsified.

Goodarzi (2006/2009) is non-negotiable — the prompt names him. His central claim is that the alliance was *strategic, not sectarian*: born in 1979–82 from concurrent shocks (Iran's revolutionary isolation, Syria's encirclement after Camp David, Iraq's invasion of Iran), and only *amplified* by sectarian instrumentalization after 2011. Students who lead with Alawite-Shia affinity will be marked down. Useful counterarguments: (1) Chatham House 2025 "shape-shifting" view that the axis was always more local than synchronized; (2) Parsi 2017 structural-realist view that Iran's posture is reactive to US containment; (3) the "always going to fall" retrospective view that the network was over-leveraged on Nasrallah and a brittle Assad.

**Common student misreading:** treating the December 2024 collapse as the result of HTS military skill. Assad fell because four scaffolds (Hezbollah, IRGC, Russian air, regime army) failed simultaneously — a subtraction story, not an HTS-victory story.

## Outline

- **Thesis.** Iran's engine ran on a strategic, not sectarian, alliance with Syria as land bridge and Hezbollah as fulcrum; the December 2024 collapse subtracted the Levantine arm but left the Iraqi-Yemeni arm intact, so Iran is structurally central but functionally diminished.
- **Body 1.** The engine pre-2024: Goodarzi's strategic alliance (1979–82 origins), Hezbollah founded 1982 with ~1,500 IRGC trainers, Soleimani's hub-and-spoke command until January 2020, "unity of the arenas" doctrine.
- **Body 2.** The 2024 subtraction: Sept 17–18 pager attacks, Sept 27 Nasrallah killed, Nov 27 Litani ceasefire, Dec 8 Damascus falls — four scaffolds (Hezbollah, IRGC, Russia/Ukraine, regime army) fail simultaneously.
- **Body 3.** Counterargument and structural-vs-functional synthesis: Chatham House "shape-shifting" critique that the axis was always more local than synchronized; rebuttal that the doctrine of "unity of the arenas" was real and is now empirically falsified, but Iraqi militias and Houthis still operate.
- **Conclusion + tie-back.** Iran remains the only actor that links the two spheres, but the linkage is thinner, more tactical, and increasingly dependent on the southern (Iraqi-Yemeni) rather than the Levantine arm.

## Sample answer

> Iran has been the structural engine of the modern Middle East regional system because it is the only actor that has connected the Israeli-Palestinian sphere and the Gulf-security sphere through a single integrated forward-defense doctrine. From 1979 onward, Tehran built a layered deterrent outward through proxies — Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Assad regime in Syria, Iraqi Shia militias post-2003, the Houthis in Yemen, and Hamas/PIJ as tactical members — that compensated for conventional inferiority and US-led containment. The December 2024 collapse of Assad did not destroy this engine, but it severed its Levantine arm and falsified the doctrine ("unity of the arenas," *wahdat al-sahat*) on which the engine's coherence had rested. The defensible synthesis is that Iran is **structurally central but functionally diminished**: still the only actor able to project pressure simultaneously into Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen, Gaza, and the Strait of Hormuz, but doing so through a thinner network whose center of gravity has shifted from Damascus and Beirut to Baghdad and Sana'a.
>
> [::: {.thesis}
> Iran's engine was structurally central before December 2024 because the Iran-Syria alliance — strategic in origin, per Goodarzi (2006) — provided the geographic land bridge linking the two regional spheres; the Assad collapse severed that bridge, leaving Iran functionally diminished but not removed.
> :::]{.thesis}
>
> The engine pre-2024 ran on three load-bearing components, all illuminated by Goodarzi's (2006) account of the Iran-Syria alliance. First, the alliance itself, which Goodarzi shows was always primarily a *strategic* balancing coalition — born in 1979–1982 from three concurrent pressures: revolutionary Iran's isolation, Hafez al-Assad's encirclement after Egypt's 1979 exit at Camp David, and Iraq's September 1980 invasion of Iran, which Syria opposed by closing the Iraqi pipeline in an extraordinary intra-Baath defection. The sectarian register (Alawite-Twelver affinity, instrumentalized later through fatwas and recruitment networks) amplified the strategic logic but did not generate it. Second, Hezbollah, founded in 1982 around roughly 1,500 IRGC trainers in the Bekaa Valley and consolidated through the catalyzing pressure of Israel's June 1982 invasion of Lebanon (Norton 2007). Hezbollah was the operational fulcrum: the actor most ideologically committed, most strategically connected to Tehran, and most capable of independent action. By the early 2020s its arsenal of roughly 120,000–150,000 rockets and missiles, including precision-guided variants, was widely considered the world's most heavily armed non-state inventory. Third, the doctrinal fusion under the slogan *wahdat al-sahat* — the claim that an Israeli action against any axis member would trigger a multi-front response. Soleimani's hub-and-spoke Quds Force command operationalized this until his killing on 3 January 2020; after that, coordination shifted toward Nasrallah personally. The engine therefore had a clear architecture: Syria as land bridge, Hezbollah as fulcrum, Iran as strategic patron, and a doctrine that turned isolated proxies into a synchronized regional capability.
>
> The December 2024 subtraction was not the result of HTS military skill. It was the simultaneous failure of four external scaffolds that had kept a hollow Syrian state upright since Russia's September 2015 intervention. The sequence ran fast: 17–18 September 2024, Israeli pager and walkie-talkie attacks decapitated Hezbollah's mid-tier command and disabled communications; 27 September 2024, the Beirut bunker strike killed Hassan Nasrallah and most of the Shura Council; 27 November 2024, the Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire codified Hezbollah's withdrawal north of the Litani; and over the next twelve days — beginning the same day, 27 November — the HTS-led Military Operations Command swept from Idlib through Aleppo (29–30 November), Hama (5 December), Homs (7 December), and Damascus (8 December). Bashar al-Assad fled to Moscow. Russia, drained by Ukraine, did not surge support; Iran, post-Soleimani and post-Nasrallah, did not surge support; the regime army, hollowed by a decade of attrition, defection, and Captagon-economy corruption, melted on contact (Lister 2024; Stimson 2025). What collapsed was not a regime defeated in battle but a security state whose external scaffolding — Hezbollah's Syrian deployment, IRGC ground presence, Russian air power — had been simultaneously degraded by the prior nine months of Israeli operations and by the Ukraine drain on Russia. The defensible reading is that the Levantine arm of Iran's engine was *subtracted*, not *defeated*.
>
> A serious counterargument deserves engagement. Mansour, Shakeri, and Haid's Chatham House (2025) "shape-shifting" framing argues that the bloc-like rendering of "the axis of resistance" overstated command coherence and understated each member's local agency: Hamas was never Iranian-controlled, the Houthis pre-existed Iranian patronage, Iraqi militias acted for parochial reasons, and the doctrine of "unity of the arenas" was always more rhetorical than operational. On this view, the 2024 collapse merely revealed what had always been true — there was no integrated engine to break, only a network of locally-rooted partners. This counterargument is partly right and partly wrong. It is right that the doctrine, when tested, did *not* produce a synchronized multi-front war: Hezbollah's October 8, 2023 "support front" was a calibrated low-grade operation that did not deploy the precision-missile arsenal; other axis members did not coordinate around Hezbollah's collapse in autumn 2024. The doctrine was empirically falsified at its first major test. But the counterargument is wrong to infer that the engine was never real. The April and October 2024 direct Iranian missile strikes on Israel — roughly 300 projectiles in April, 200 ballistic missiles in October — were unprecedented escalations that only made strategic sense within an integrated forward-defense architecture; the cumulative Iranian financial commitment to Syria of $30–50 billion (Carnegie 2024) is hard to read as anything other than treating Damascus as a strategic asset; and the *speed* with which the absence of Hezbollah/IRGC presence in Syria translated into the regime's collapse is itself evidence that the scaffolding had been load-bearing. The synthesis is therefore that the doctrine was real and is now broken; the network was integrated and is now disaggregating.
>
> What survives is structural, not functional. Iran remains the only regional actor able to project pressure simultaneously into Lebanon (residual Hezbollah, ~100,000 fighters surviving but without precision deterrent), Iraq (Kata'ib Hezbollah, AAH, the broader PMF), Yemen (the Houthis, who continued Red Sea attacks through 2025), Gaza (Hamas/PIJ as tactical partners), and the Strait of Hormuz (IRGC Navy harassment posture). The June 13–24, 2025 Twelve-Day War — Israel's Operation Rising Lion, US strikes on Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan on 22 June, and Iran's 550+ ballistic missile and ~1,000 drone response — demonstrated both that Iran's deterrence-by-distance had collapsed and that Iran could still impose substantial costs. Soufan Center (2025) and Stimson (2025) converge on the assessment that the axis is "down but not out": Iraqi militias and the Houthis have, in fact, become *more* central in Iranian planning post-2024, and Iran's nuclear program (with 60% HEU stockpile retained) functions as the residual deterrent the proxy network can no longer provide.
>
> Iran is therefore still the engine, but it is now an engine without its Levantine drive train. The structural argument — that Iran is the only actor linking the two spheres — survives the Assad collapse. The functional reality — that the linkage runs as thickly as it did before — does not. The throughline holds: Iran connected the Gulf-security sphere to the Israeli sphere through Hezbollah and Syria from 1982 through 2024, and even in the engine's degraded form, Iraqi missile platforms and Houthi missiles in the Bab al-Mandeb continue to do the linkage work that Hezbollah's southern Lebanon arsenal once did alone.

## Grading rubric — what an A vs. C answer looks like

| Dimension | A-grade | C-grade |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis | Distinguishes structural centrality from functional diminishment | "Iran is still important" with no axis on which to judge |
| Evidence density | 1979, 1982, 1/3/2020, 9/17–18/24, 9/27/24, 11/27/24, 12/8/24, 6/13–24/25 — eight or more specific dates | Two or three vague dates; "after Assad fell" |
| Frame integration | (Goodarzi 2006) used for the strategic-not-sectarian claim; (Norton 2007) for Hezbollah; Chatham House 2025 as counter | Goodarzi mentioned but not deployed; sectarian framing leads |
| Counterargument | Engages Chatham House "shape-shifting" view and rebuts via April/Oct 2024 strikes + funding scale | No counterargument, or "some scholars disagree" wave-off |
| Tie-back | Final sentence connects to Iran-as-engine throughline as a still-true structural claim | Ends with summary, no throughline tie |

# Prompt 3 — The Carousel

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Prompt.** Apply a Nash-equilibrium framing to the Middle East regional system as it stood in October 2023. Identify the four key but not equal actors, their best-response strategies, and at least three exit conditions under which the equilibrium could shift. How does October 7 fit into this framework — as shock, deviation, or equilibrium-preserving event?
:::

## Decoder

The prompt names the framework (Nash) and demands four operations: (1) define the equilibrium, (2) name the actors and their strategies, (3) identify exit conditions, and (4) classify October 7. The cleanest cut on (4) is to argue October 7 was a **deviation** that triggered a **shock** to the matrix without (yet) producing a new stable equilibrium — a deviation the deviator could not afford in expected-value terms but that nonetheless reshaped subsequent best responses across the system.

The "four key but not equal actors" formulation is Hammad's directly: Israel, Palestinian factions (Hamas + PA, bifurcated), Iran, Saudi/Gulf, with the US as the structural fifth actor whose presence sets the payoff matrix. Strategies must be *best responses given the others' strategies* — that is the formal NE definition (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994).

Frames most useful: Schelling (1960) on coordination and tacit rules, Fearon (1995) on commitment problems and private information as the three rationalist causes of war, Jervis (1978) on the security dilemma, Walt (1996) on revolutions reshaping equilibria. The exam answer should be tight on the formal definition before doing applied work.

**Common student misreading:** treating Nash equilibrium as a synonym for "stalemate." NE is not a moral judgment; it is a strategic-consistency claim. A bloody system can be in equilibrium; a peaceful one can be out of it.

## Outline

- **Thesis.** The October 2023 system was a stable Nash equilibrium because each actor's strategy was a best response to every other's; October 7 was a deviation triggered by Hamas's payoff calculation but with a destabilizing cascade that altered the matrix faster than a new equilibrium could form.
- **Body 1.** Formal NE definition + four-actor mapping: Israel (security maximalism + nuclear ambiguity), Palestinian factions (split: Hamas armed resistance, PA accommodation), Iran (forward defense via proxies + nuclear hedging), Saudi/Gulf (regime survival + Iran balance + selective normalization). US as fifth structural actor.
- **Body 2.** Three exit conditions: (i) exogenous shock that changes payoffs (1979, 2011, 2024 Assad); (ii) hegemonic intervention altering bargaining range (Camp David 1978, Oslo 1993, Accords 2020); (iii) coalition shift / great-power realignment (March 2023 Beijing-brokered Saudi-Iran restoration). Costly-signal mechanism (Sadat 1977) as bonus fourth.
- **Body 3.** October 7 classification: deviation (Hamas's "extraordinary act" against expected payoffs) that triggered a shock cascade (Hezbollah front, Saudi pause, Hezbollah destruction Sept–Nov 2024, Assad collapse Dec 2024), reshaping payoffs faster than equilibration could occur.
- **Conclusion + tie-back.** The carousel rotates within an equilibrium; October 7 was the moment the rotation hit a structural edge and the underlying matrix began to change.

## Sample answer

> A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which no player can unilaterally deviate and improve her payoff, holding every other player's strategy fixed (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994). The Middle East regional system as it stood on 6 October 2023 satisfied this definition exactly: Israel, the Palestinian factions, Iran, and Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states were each playing best responses given the others' strategies, with the United States as a structural fifth actor whose presence and security guarantees set the payoff matrix. The result was the configuration Hammad calls the carousel — episodes of escalation and de-escalation that rotate the surface of the system without changing the underlying strategy profile. October 7 is best classified as a **deviation** by one actor (Hamas) whose individual best-response calculation was tight, ambiguous, or arguably miscalculated, but which triggered a **shock cascade** that has altered the payoff matrix faster than a new stable equilibrium can form. The system in May 2026 is therefore between equilibria — the old one disrupted, the next one not yet visible.
>
> [::: {.thesis}
> The October 2023 regional system was a stable Nash equilibrium of best responses; October 7 was a deviation that triggered a payoff-shock cascade, leaving the system in 2026 between equilibria rather than at a new one.
> :::]{.thesis}
>
> The four key but not equal actors and their best-response strategies map onto the system as follows. **Israel's** strategy is security maximalism plus nuclear ambiguity, anchored in what Shlaim (2000) calls the Iron Wall logic: only demonstrated unbreakable strength produces Arab acceptance. Its source of leverage is military primacy, US alignment, and the technology sector; its constraint is domestic coalition fragility and demographic squeeze. Given every other actor's strategy, unilateral concession on settlements or Palestinian statehood would be electorally fatal and strategically risky — so the best response is to maintain the status quo and respond to provocations with overwhelming force. **The Palestinian factions** are themselves in an internal equilibrium. Hamas pursues armed resistance partly because it cannot credibly commit to long peace without losing legitimacy to harder factions; the PA in Ramallah accommodates partly because security cooperation with Israel is the price of its survival. The Hamas-PA divide is a stable internal NE: each faction's continuance depends on the other not disappearing. **Iran's** strategy is forward defense through proxies — Hezbollah, Iraqi militias, the Houthis, Hamas/PIJ as tactical partners, and (until December 2024) the Assad regime as the geographic hinge — plus nuclear hedging. Conventional parity with Israel and the US is impossible, so asymmetric and stand-off capabilities are Iran's best response (Ostovar 2016). **Saudi Arabia and the Gulf** treat regime survival as the master variable, balancing Iran via US security guarantees and selective Israeli cooperation, hedging between Washington and Beijing — the China-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement of 10 March 2023 is the visible result of that hedge. The **United States** is a structural fifth actor whose presence creates the payoff matrix in which all of the above are best responses; remove it, and many of the strategies become incoherent.
>
> Three exit conditions can shift this equilibrium, each with a clear historical instance. First, **exogenous shocks that change payoffs**: the February 1979 Iranian Revolution converted Iran from Israeli partner to leading revisionist; the 2011 Arab Spring temporarily destabilized Egypt, Syria, Libya, Yemen; the 8 December 2024 collapse of Assad — itself enabled by Israel's degradation of Hezbollah from 17 September through 27 November 2024 and by Russian distraction in Ukraine — broke Iran's land bridge to Lebanon. Second, **hegemonic intervention that alters the bargaining range**: Camp David 1978 (Carter brokering Egypt-Israel) removed the largest Arab military from the equilibrium; Oslo 1993 created the Palestinian Authority; the Abraham Accords of August–December 2020 pulled UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco into formal relations with Israel without resolving the Palestinian core. Third, **coalition shifts and great-power realignment**: the 10 March 2023 China-mediated Saudi-Iran restoration introduced Beijing as a face-saving guarantor, partly substituting for the US security backstop. A bonus fourth mechanism — **new information that resolves commitment problems** — Fearon (1995) identifies as the deepest rationalist barrier to peace; Sadat's 1977 Jerusalem visit was the canonical costly signal that no private channel could have produced.
>
> Where does October 7 fit? The most defensible classification is that it was a **deviation by Hamas** that produced a **shock cascade** large enough to reshape several actors' best responses but not large enough to produce a new equilibrium yet. The deviation reading is supported by three pieces of evidence. First, captured Hamas internal documents from 2022–23 and Sinwar communications dated late September 2023 (with caveats about Israeli intelligence provenance) suggest derailing Saudi-Israel normalization was at minimum one strategic motivation; the spoiler theory is more plausible than not. Second, the operational scale — roughly 1,200 Israeli dead, ~250 hostages — was an order of magnitude beyond previous escalations and falls outside the bandwidth of the carousel's prior rotation. Third, Hamas's expected-value calculation, given an overwhelming Israeli response, was tight: the deviation made sense only if it succeeded in generating regional cascade effects (Hezbollah front, Saudi pause, axis activation) that compensated for the certain Israeli counter-strike. Whether one judges the calculation correct depends on one's prior about Iran's regional position in 2026 — a Tehran view sees the spoiler succeed (Saudi normalization paused, Israel diplomatically isolated), an Israeli view sees the spoiler fail (Hamas decapitated, Hezbollah broken, Assad fallen, Iran struck directly).
>
> One might object — as constructivists like Wendt (1999) do — that NE framing presupposes given preferences and rational calculation, and that the Israel-Palestine conflict is over competing identity narratives that game theory cannot capture. The objection is real but does not rescue an alternative model from explanatory burden. NE describes the *structure of strategic incentives* given preferences; constructivism explains why those preferences are what they are. Both can be true. A second objection — Mitchell's (2011) structural-economic critique — would emphasize that the payoff matrix is itself a product of oil rents, the dollar-recycling system, and US arms transfers, so reading the system as a game of states obscures the political economy. Again, both can be true: the political economy *constitutes* the matrix; the game theory *describes the strategy profile* on that matrix.
>
> By May 2026, the matrix is visibly altered. Hezbollah's deterrent value to Iran is broken; Assad is gone; the US has bombed Iranian nuclear sites in the June 2025 Twelve-Day War; Saudi Arabia has restored Palestinian-state conditionality on any normalization; China has entered as a hedging guarantor. None of these were features of the October 6, 2023 equilibrium. Yet a new stable equilibrium has not formed: Iran's regional architecture is degraded but not eliminated, the Sharaa government in Damascus is contested, the Saudi track is in deep freeze rather than revived. The carousel rotated for two decades. October 7 was the moment the rotation hit a structural edge and the underlying matrix began to change. The throughline survives: Nash equilibrium explains why nothing changes on its own and what kind of shock is required to force change — and the shock has now, in fact, arrived.

## Grading rubric — what an A vs. C answer looks like

| Dimension | A-grade | C-grade |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis | Classifies Oct 7 as deviation triggering shock cascade, distinguishes "between equilibria" from "new equilibrium" | "October 7 changed everything" with no formal classification |
| Evidence density | Formal NE definition + four actors + three (or four) exit conditions with dated examples (1978, 1993, 2020, 3/23, 12/24) | Vague invocation of "game theory" without formal apparatus |
| Frame integration | (Osborne & Rubinstein 1994) for definition, (Schelling 1960), (Fearon 1995), (Shlaim 2000), (Wendt 1999) as objection | "Game theorists say…" without authors or operative claims |
| Counterargument | Engages constructivist (Wendt) and/or structural-economic (Mitchell) objection, rebuts via complementarity | No objection, or one-sentence dismissal |
| Tie-back | Final sentence connects to Nash carousel throughline as the master frame | Ends with restatement of thesis |

# Prompt 4 — The Robust State

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Prompt.** Why did the 2011 Arab Spring produce sustained democratic transition in Tunisia but reversion or repression elsewhere? Use Bellin (2004) and Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds (2015) as your primary frames. Address the December 2024 Syrian collapse as a delayed-onset case that complicates the Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds typology.
:::

## Decoder

This is a comparative-authoritarianism prompt with a twist: the twist is the December 2024 Syria collapse, which arrives 13 years late and demands engagement with whether the Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds (BMR) two-variable typology — hereditary executive AND oil rents predict regime survival — can absorb a delayed transition that began as a transition-blockage and ended as a regime collapse 13 years later.

Bellin (2004) is the coercive-apparatus argument: regimes survive when their security forces are patrimonially organized, well-financed by rents, internationally supported, and facing low-mobilization populations. BMR (2015) reduces this to two variables: a hereditary executive (the regime's survival is bound to a family) AND oil rents (resources buy off and coerce). Tunisia had neither — Ben Ali was a rotating-presidency dictator, not a dynasty, and Tunisia is not an oil state — so it transitioned. Egypt had hereditary tendencies (Mubarak's son) but no oil; transition started, then was reversed by Sisi's 2013 coup. Bahrain had a dynasty plus Gulf cover; uprising was crushed by Peninsula Shield in March 2011. Syria had a dynasty (Bashar succeeded Hafez in 2000) but only modest oil; survived 13 years against worse odds, then fell when the *external* scaffolding (Hezbollah, IRGC, Russia, regime army) was subtracted simultaneously in late 2024.

The BMR typology predicts Syria should have *survived*; the fact that it did, for 13 years, validates the typology's short-run predictive power, but the December 2024 collapse complicates the typology by showing that a regime can survive its own internal mobilization and still fall to *external scaffolding subtraction* — a mechanism BMR's two-variable model does not theorize.

**Common student misreading:** treating Syria 2024 as a "second wave" of the Arab Spring. It was not — it was the result of Israeli/Russian shocks to Iran's regional posture, not domestic mobilization.

## Outline

- **Thesis.** Bellin and BMR explain the cross-sectional variation in 2011 outcomes well, but the Syria 2024 case requires augmenting BMR's hereditary-executive-plus-rents typology with an external-scaffolding variable: regimes that depend on foreign coercive subsidy can collapse when that subsidy fails simultaneously, even with hereditary structure intact.
- **Body 1.** The 2011 sorting: Tunisia (no dynasty, no rents → transition); Egypt (mild hereditary, no rents → transition then 2013 reversion under Sisi, with Sayigh's military-economy explanation); Bahrain (dynasty + Gulf cover → crushed by Peninsula Shield, March 2011); Libya (dynasty + rents but eccentric coercive apparatus → external intervention).
- **Body 2.** Syria 2011–2024 as BMR validation: hereditary executive (Bashar succeeded Hafez 2000) + modest rents + intensely patrimonial coercive apparatus (Bellin's four overlapping mukhabarat) + Iran/Hezbollah/Russia external scaffolding → survived against worse odds than any other Arab Spring regime.
- **Body 3.** The 2024 collapse as typology-complicating: not a domestic-mobilization story but an external-scaffolding-subtraction story (Hezbollah Sept–Nov 2024, IRGC, Russia/Ukraine, regime army), 12 days from Idlib offensive to Damascus fall — augmentation needed, not refutation.
- **Conclusion + tie-back.** Authoritarian robustness depends on coercive apparatus + rents + dynasty + external subsidy; remove any one and survival is harder, but the four can substitute for each other in the short run.

## Sample answer

> The 2011 Arab Spring produced sustained democratic transition in Tunisia and reversion or repression nearly everywhere else because authoritarian survival in MENA depends on the structural conditions of the coercive apparatus rather than on the size or moral force of street mobilization. Bellin's (2004; 2012) framework specifies four conditions for the robustness of an authoritarian regime: a coercive apparatus that is patrimonially organized rather than institutionalized, well-financed by rents, internationally supported, and facing low-mobilization populations. Brownlee, Masoud, and Reynolds (2015) compress this into a two-variable typology — hereditary executive AND oil rents — that predicts which Arab Spring states transitioned and which did not. The typology fits Tunisia, Egypt, Bahrain, and Libya. It also fits Syria for the first thirteen years after the 2011 uprising began, when Bashar al-Assad's regime survived intense internal mobilization that the BMR variables predicted it should survive. The December 2024 collapse — fast, total, and produced by the simultaneous subtraction of *external* scaffolding rather than internal cracking — complicates BMR by showing that the typology's two variables describe necessary conditions for short-run survival but are not sufficient to predict long-run trajectory once external coercive subsidy fails.
>
> [::: {.thesis}
> Bellin and BMR explain the 2011 cross-sectional sorting; Syria 2024 augments rather than refutes the typology by showing that external coercive scaffolding is a third variable whose simultaneous failure can collapse an otherwise BMR-predicted-to-survive regime.
> :::]{.thesis}
>
> The 2011 sorting tracks Bellin's and BMR's variables closely. Tunisia's Ben Ali was a rotating-presidency dictator without a hereditary lineage; Tunisia is not an oil state; the coercive apparatus was institutionalized rather than patrimonial; the army declined to fire on protesters in mid-January 2011 and Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011. The transition produced a 2014 constitution and successive elections, even with substantial backsliding under Saied after 2021. Egypt's Mubarak was building a hereditary track for his son Gamal but had not consummated it; Egypt has limited oil rents; the army's response in 2011 was institutionally complex — it eased Mubarak out on 11 February 2011, allowed elections, and then in July 2013 Sisi's coup reversed the transition. Sayigh (2019) explains the Egyptian reversion through the lens of military economy: when the Egyptian armed forces run roughly 25% of government spending, liberalization is an existential threat to the officer corps, and the coup is rational from inside the apparatus. Bahrain's Khalifa dynasty plus Gulf cover produced the predicted survival outcome: the uprising at Pearl Roundabout was crushed in March 2011 by the Peninsula Shield Force, with Saudi armored units crossing the King Fahd Causeway. Libya — dynasty (the Gaddafi family) plus rents (oil) — should have survived per BMR, but the eccentric structure of Gaddafi's coercive apparatus and the March 2011 NATO intervention produced an externally-imposed transition that subsequently fragmented. The four cases align well: Tunisia (no dynasty, no rents → transition), Egypt (mild dynasty, no rents → transition then reversion via military-economy logic), Bahrain (dynasty + Gulf cover → crushed), Libya (dynasty + rents → externally toppled, then collapsed).
>
> Syria 2011–2024 is the BMR typology's strongest test, and for thirteen years it confirmed the typology against worse odds than any other case. Bashar succeeded his father Hafez in July 2000 — a clean hereditary transition. Syria has modest oil rents (sufficient before sanctions to subsidize the coercive apparatus, hollowed by 2018 but partly substituted by Iranian credit). The coercive apparatus was the textbook Bellin case: four overlapping mukhabarat (Military Intelligence, Air Force Intelligence, General Security, Political Security), patrimonially staffed with Alawite kin networks at sensitive command nodes, internationally supported by Iran (IRGC, Hezbollah from 2013 openly, foreign Shia militias including Liwa Fatemiyoun and Liwa Zaynabiyoun) and from September 2015 by Russian air power. Cumulative Iranian financial commitment to Assad ran $30–50 billion (Carnegie 2024). The 2011 uprising was severe — the Daraa protests of March 2011 escalated into a full civil war by 2012 — but the apparatus did not crack from within: senior Alawite officers did not defect at scale, the welding of regime survival to personal loyalty held, and the Russian intervention of September 2015 reversed the regime's strategic decline. By 2019, the regime had reconquered most of the country except Idlib (HTS), the northeast (SDF), and the Turkish-occupied northern strip. By May 2023, Syria was readmitted to the Arab League. BMR's two variables — hereditary executive plus rents (broadly construed to include external coercive subsidy as a rent-substitute) — held up.
>
> The December 2024 collapse complicates the typology not by refuting it but by exposing what it does not theorize. The collapse was fast — twelve days from the 27 November 2024 HTS-led "Deterrence of Aggression" offensive to the 8 December 2024 fall of Damascus, with Aleppo, Hama, and Homs in between. Assad fled to Moscow. The mechanism was not internal mobilization, which had largely been suppressed for a decade. It was the simultaneous subtraction of all four external scaffolds: Hezbollah devastated by the Israeli campaign of September–November 2024 (pager attacks 17–18 September, Nasrallah killed 27 September, Litani ceasefire 27 November); IRGC leadership and air defenses degraded by Israeli strikes through the spring and summer of 2024; Russia drained by Ukraine and unable to surge a 2015-style intervention; and the regime army hollowed by a decade of attrition, defection, salary collapse, and Captagon-economy corruption (Lister 2024; ICG 2024). Frontline units melted on contact. The regime did not lose a battle; it lost its propping.
>
> One might object that this is just BMR's "international support" variable doing its work — that Syria's apparent survival from 2011 to 2024 was always conditional on external subsidy, and the collapse confirms rather than complicates the typology. The objection is half-right and half-wrong. It is right that BMR allows external support to enter as one of the conditions; it is wrong to treat that variable as on a par with the hereditary-executive and rents variables. The simultaneous-subtraction mechanism — four scaffolds failing in the same six-month window — has a different theoretical structure from a slow erosion of any single variable. It is closer to what Walt (1996) calls a revolution-equivalent shock, in which the cost-balance of the equilibrium changes faster than actors can re-equilibrate. A regime that survives slow attrition can collapse to a fast simultaneous subtraction even with its core BMR variables (dynasty, rents) intact. The typology's two variables describe necessary conditions for short-run survival; they understate the joint-failure-mode risk for regimes whose coercive apparatus has become structurally dependent on external subsidy.
>
> Tunisia's continued (if eroded) democratic order, Egypt's military-economy reversion, Bahrain's Gulf-cover crushing, and Syria's thirteen-year survival followed by 2024 collapse are all consistent with Bellin's framework once external coercive subsidy is treated as a substitutable but joint-failure-vulnerable input alongside hereditary executive and rents. Authoritarian robustness in MENA depends on a coercive apparatus and rentier resources, but the supply chain of that robustness is more fragile than the BMR typology suggests when external scaffolding becomes load-bearing. That is the throughline this prompt connects to: the same regime-public delinking that lets Gulf monarchies sign the Abraham Accords without electoral cost is what lets Bashar suppress Syrian society for thirteen years without internal cracking — and the same external dependence that lets him do it is what subtracts in December 2024 when Iran's regional engine is broken at the Levantine end.

## Grading rubric — what an A vs. C answer looks like

| Dimension | A-grade | C-grade |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis | Augments BMR with external-scaffolding variable; classifies Syria 2024 as joint-failure-mode case | "Bellin and BMR explain Arab Spring outcomes" with no augmentation |
| Evidence density | 1/14/2011 (Ben Ali), 2/11/2011 (Mubarak), 3/2011 (Peninsula Shield), 7/2013 (Sisi), 9/2015 (Russia), 11/27–12/8/2024 (HTS offensive) | "The Arab Spring" with no specific dates |
| Frame integration | (Bellin 2004) operative claim; (Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds 2015) two-variable typology; (Sayigh 2019) for Egypt; (Walt 1996) for shock theory | Authors named without operative claims |
| Counterargument | Engages "BMR already includes international support" objection; rebuts via simultaneous-subtraction mechanism | No counterargument |
| Tie-back | Connects to throughline (regime-public delinking + external dependence) | Ends with restatement |

# Prompt 5 — The System

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Prompt.** F. Gregory Gause III argues the United States has had primacy and unipolarity in the Middle East but never hegemony. Defend or contest this claim using evidence from 2003 to 2026. How does the Saudi-Iran rapprochement of March 2023 figure into your answer?
:::

## Decoder

The prompt names Gause's threefold distinction (primacy ≠ unipolarity ≠ hegemony) and demands a defense or contest. Gause's operative definitions: *primacy* = being the most powerful actor; *unipolarity* = having no peer competitor; *hegemony* = the ability to dictate outcomes through accepted leadership. The US has had primacy (largest military, most-deployed, primary security guarantor for several states) and unipolarity (no peer in the regional theater) since the early 1990s, but not hegemony (its preferred outcomes have been routinely defied — most starkly by Iran since 1979, by Hamas since 2007, by Saudi-Iran 2023, by the Houthis throughout, and by the Iraqi insurgency it created in 2003).

The defensible answer **defends** the distinction. The 2003 Iraq invasion is the showcase: the US could occupy Baghdad (primacy and unipolarity in raw power) but could not produce its preferred outcome (a stable, pro-American, non-Iranian-influenced Iraq), because Iran exploited the opening — Vali Nasr's "Shia Revival" thesis. The March 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement, brokered in Beijing, is the second major piece of evidence: a critical regional security accord was mediated by China, with Oman and Iraq doing prior groundwork — without significant US involvement.

Frames most useful: Gause directly, Mitchell (2011) on infrastructure shaping politics (oil infrastructure makes the US's regional role primarily extractive and security-guaranteeing rather than nation-building), and Walt (1996) on alliances reshaping under shock.

**Common student misreading:** conflating *withdrawal* (which the US has not done) with *loss of hegemony* (which it never had). Trump 2.0 is pursuing renewed engagement, including the November 2025 Kazakhstan accession to the Accords and the Twelve-Day War strikes — primacy continues; hegemony was never on offer.

## Outline

- **Thesis.** Defend Gause's distinction: from 2003 to 2026 the US has retained primacy and unipolarity but never achieved hegemony, and the March 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement crystallizes the difference by showing that Beijing — not Washington — brokered a critical regional security agreement.
- **Body 1.** Gause's definitions + 2003 Iraq as showcase: occupation succeeded in raw-power terms (primacy/unipolarity) but produced the opposite of preferred outcome (Iranian regional opening, "Shia Revival" per Nasr).
- **Body 2.** 2003–2023 cumulative defiance: Hamas 2007 takeover of Gaza, Iran's regional expansion through Syria/Iraq/Lebanon/Yemen, 2011 Arab Spring outcomes the US did not control, JCPOA negotiated by P5+1 (signaling shared rather than hegemonic order), 2018 withdrawal followed by Iranian breakout, the Aramco strikes of September 2019.
- **Body 3.** The 10 March 2023 Beijing-mediated Saudi-Iran agreement as the crystallizing moment: critical regional security accord, brokered by Beijing rather than Washington, with Oman and Iraq doing prior groundwork; survives Assad's December 2024 fall, the June 2025 Twelve-Day War. Counterargument: US still primary (Twelve-Day War strikes, F-35 sale, defense pacts under negotiation) — rebuttal: that's primacy, not hegemony.
- **Conclusion + tie-back.** Hegemony was never on offer; primacy continues; the 2023 Beijing brokerage is not US "loss" but the visible reality that hegemony was never the regional structure.

## Sample answer

> F. Gregory Gause III's distinction among primacy, unipolarity, and hegemony is among the most useful analytical contributions in recent Middle East scholarship because it captures what every careful observer of the post-2003 region has known but few have stated cleanly: the United States has been the most powerful regional actor and has had no peer competitor for two decades, but its preferred outcomes have been defied with such regularity that calling its position "hegemonic" misdescribes the order. Primacy means being the strongest; unipolarity means having no rival of comparable weight; hegemony means the ability to set the terms others accept. The US has had the first two since at least the early 1990s and certainly since the Soviet collapse. It has never had the third. The 10 March 2023 Beijing-mediated Saudi-Iran rapprochement is the cleanest single piece of evidence for this proposition, because it is the moment a critical regional security agreement was brokered by Beijing rather than Washington — and it survived every subsequent shock, from the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack through the December 2024 collapse of Assad to the June 2025 Twelve-Day War. The defensible thesis is therefore to defend Gause's distinction.
>
> [::: {.thesis}
> The US has retained primacy and unipolarity from 2003 to 2026 but never achieved hegemony; the March 2023 Beijing-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement is the clearest visible evidence that the regional security architecture has never been hegemonically Washington-set.
> :::]{.thesis}
>
> The 2003 Iraq invasion is the showcase test case for Gause's distinction. The US could project overwhelming conventional force — Baghdad fell on 9 April 2003, the regime was decapitated, occupation forces were established at scale. That is primacy and unipolarity in raw power terms; no other regional or global actor could have done the same operation. Yet the *outcome* the invasion produced was the opposite of the preferred US outcome. Coalition Provisional Authority decisions in 2003–2004 — the de-Ba'athification order, the dissolution of the Iraqi army, the abrupt loss of administrative capacity — combined with structural conditions to produce a Shia-majority political order whose closest external sponsor was Tehran rather than Washington. Vali Nasr's *Shia Revival* (2007) thesis frames this directly: the 2003 invasion unintentionally empowered Iran's Shia Iraqi allies (SCIRI, Dawa, Sadrists, the militias that would eventually become Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq under the broader PMF), and Iran emerged from the post-Saddam moment with deeper regional reach than at any time since the 1979 revolution. The US occupied; Iran benefited. Hegemony — if it existed — would have produced the US-preferred outcome. It did not.
>
> The pattern of primacy-without-hegemony repeats across two decades. In June 2007 Hamas took military control of Gaza, displacing the PA in defiance of US-led conditions; the US could not reverse this. From 2011 onward, the Arab Spring outcomes the US did not control: Tunisia transitioned without significant US brokerage, Egypt's 2011 transition was reversed by Sisi's July 2013 coup that the US ultimately accommodated, Bahrain's protests were crushed by Saudi-led Peninsula Shield forces in March 2011 over US discomfort, and Libya's 2011 NATO intervention produced state collapse rather than the US-preferred ordered transition. The July 2015 JCPOA was negotiated by the P5+1, not by the US alone, signaling a shared-rather-than-hegemonic regional order; Trump's May 2018 withdrawal failed to achieve its objectives — Iran did not return to the table on US terms, instead beginning a phased nuclear breakout that culminated in the 60% HEU stockpile retained through 2026. The September 2019 Aramco strikes, attributed to Iran or Iranian-aligned actors, were not deterred by US presence in the Gulf; the US response was rhetorical rather than kinetic. Each of these events is consistent with primacy and unipolarity (the US remains the most powerful actor and has no regional peer) but inconsistent with hegemony (preferred outcomes routinely defied).
>
> The 10 March 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement crystallizes the structural reality. The agreement restored diplomatic ties between Riyadh and Tehran after a seven-year rupture, with Iraq and Oman doing extensive prior groundwork and the Chinese announcement providing the closing platform. The brokerage was Beijing's. Washington was not absent — it was *bypassed*, in the precise sense that two of its most important regional partners chose to formalize a security agreement under another great power's auspices. Atlantic Council (2024) and Carnegie (2023) accounts converge on the assessment that Saudi Arabia's motivations included both Iran-balancing and *hedging against US strategic reliability*, especially after the 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal. The agreement has survived every subsequent shock that observers expected to break it: Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack, the Israeli destruction of Hezbollah leadership in autumn 2024, the 8 December 2024 collapse of Assad, the June 2025 Twelve-Day War. A hegemonic US would have either prevented the rapprochement or restructured it under American auspices; primacy alone explains the actual trajectory.
>
> A serious counterargument is that the US has, in fact, exercised something close to hegemony in the period since 2024 — Trump 2.0's renewed Accords expansion, the November 2025 announced Kazakhstan accession, the US bombing of Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan on 22 June 2025 in coordination with Israeli strikes, the brokered 24 June 2025 ceasefire, the November 2025 sanctions waivers and Caesar Act repeal in the Sharaa case, the 14-point US-brokered SDF-Damascus deal of late 2025. This is, the objection runs, hegemony in operation. The objection misreads the cases. Each of those instances is consistent with *primacy* — the US is the most powerful actor and can act decisively when it chooses — but each is also limited in ways that hegemony would not be. The Twelve-Day War strikes did not eliminate Iran's nuclear program (the 60% HEU stockpile remains, and Pakistani-mediated negotiations continued through 2026). The Accords expansion has not produced Saudi accession. The Caesar Act repeal acknowledged a Sharaa transition that the US did not engineer. The SDF-Damascus deal codified terms set substantially by Damascus rather than Washington. Mitchell's (2011) framing in *Carbon Democracy* points to the deeper reason: US infrastructure-political role in the region is primarily extractive and security-guaranteeing rather than nation-shaping, which constrains hegemony from the outset. Walt's (1996) work on revolutions and alliances suggests that periods of regional shock — and 2024–26 is rich in them — tend to clarify rather than obscure the limits of any external power's control.
>
> The defensible synthesis is therefore to *defend* Gause's distinction. The US has had primacy and unipolarity in the Middle East from 2003 to 2026 — by every conventional metric of power projection, alliance density, and military deployment, no actor approaches it. It has not had hegemony, because its preferred outcomes have been defied with sufficient regularity to make the descriptor inappropriate, and the regional security architecture has, since at least 2023, included Beijing as a face-saving guarantor for agreements among Washington's nominal partners. The Saudi-Iran rapprochement is not a story of US "loss" — that frame imports the assumption of prior hegemony. It is the story of what the regional order has always been: a system in which the US is structurally central but never structurally determinative, in which primacy survives every individual setback but hegemony was never the operative concept. The throughline this connects to is the Nash equilibrium: the US is the structural fifth actor whose presence sets the payoff matrix, but the equilibrium itself is produced by the best responses of regional players, not by hegemonic dictation. That is what Gause has been arguing all along.

## Grading rubric — what an A vs. C answer looks like

| Dimension | A-grade | C-grade |
|---|---|---|
| Thesis | Defends Gause's three-way distinction; classifies 2023 Beijing brokerage as evidence of structural reality, not "loss" | "The US is declining in the Middle East" without Gause's distinction |
| Evidence density | 4/9/03 Baghdad falls, 6/07 Hamas Gaza takeover, 7/2015 JCPOA, 5/2018 withdrawal, 9/2019 Aramco, 3/10/23 Beijing, 6/22/25 US strikes | Vague "throughout the post-2003 period" |
| Frame integration | (Gause 2024) operative definitions; (Nasr 2007) Shia Revival; (Mitchell 2011) infrastructure logic; (Walt 1996) shock | Gause named without his definitions deployed |
| Counterargument | Engages "Trump 2.0 = hegemony" objection; rebuts via Iran nuclear residual + Saudi non-accession + Caesar Act context | No counterargument |
| Tie-back | Connects Gause's distinction to Nash carousel throughline (US as structural fifth actor) | Ends with restatement |

## 10 essay-bank one-liners — adapt under time pressure

::: {.callout-tip}
**These are pre-built thesis statements distinct from the five in the cram sheet.** Memorize two or three; in the exam, twist whichever fits the prompt's verb. The shape is: structural claim + named author/frame + dated evidence + tie-back signal.
:::

1. The Abraham Accords were premised on a regime-public delinking wager (Lynch 2024) that Arab Barometer 2024 falsified — Saudi opposition to normalization rose from 38% to 68% in eighteen months — and the wager's failure is what made Riyadh re-attach Palestinian-state conditionality after October 7.
2. Iran's regional engine ran on a strategic, not sectarian, alliance with Syria (Goodarzi 2006), and the December 2024 Damascus collapse subtracted the geographic land bridge without eliminating the Iraqi and Yemeni arms — leaving Iran structurally central but functionally diminished.
3. The Bellin (2004) coercive-apparatus framework predicted Bahrain's March 2011 crushing and Tunisia's January 2011 transition with equal accuracy because it specifies the patrimonial-versus-institutional distinction that BMR's two-variable typology compresses.
4. The Brownlee/Masoud/Reynolds (2015) typology requires augmentation by an external-scaffolding variable to explain why Syria survived its own population for thirteen years and then collapsed in twelve days when four foreign props failed simultaneously.
5. Mitchell's (2011) *Carbon Democracy* thesis explains why US regional involvement has always been extractive-and-guaranteeing rather than transformational, which is the structural reason the US has had primacy without hegemony in Gause's (2024) sense.
6. The October 7, 2023 Hamas attack is best classified, in Nash-equilibrium terms, as a deviation whose expected-value calculation depended on triggering a regional cascade — a calculation that Tehran benefited from ex post but did not engineer ex ante.
7. The 10 March 2023 Beijing-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement is the single clearest piece of evidence that the regional security architecture has never been hegemonically Washington-set, because a critical agreement was mediated by China and survived every subsequent regional shock.
8. The doctrine of *wahdat al-sahat* ("unity of the arenas") was empirically falsified between October 2023 and December 2024: Hezbollah did not deploy its precision arsenal, other axis members did not synchronize defense of Hezbollah, and the simultaneous-failure cascade ended Iran's land-bridge architecture.
9. Sayigh's (2019) account of Egypt's military-economy — roughly a quarter of government spending under armed-forces control — explains why the 2013 Sisi coup was rational from inside the apparatus and why no Bellin-robust military will accept a transition that liberalizes its rents.
10. The carousel rotates within a Nash equilibrium because each actor's strategy is a best response to every other actor's strategy (Osborne and Rubinstein 1994); only payoff-matrix shocks — 1979, 2003, 2011, 2023, 2024 — produce real shifts, and 2024 is the shock-richest year since 1979.

## Things Hammad penalizes — six common errors with concrete examples

::: {.callout-warning}
**These are the moves that tank otherwise competent essays.** Watch for them in your own outline before you start writing.
:::

1. **Sectarian-first framing of the Iran-Syria alliance.** "The Iran-Syria alliance was driven by Shia solidarity." Wrong frame; Goodarzi (2006) is explicit that the alliance was strategic, with the sectarian register *amplifying* but not generating it. The right move is strategic-first, sectarian-as-instrumental.
2. **Treating the Abraham Accords as a regional architecture.** "The Accords created a new Middle East regional order." Wrong scale. The Accords are four bilateral deals; Saudi never signed; the architecture claim was Trump-administration framing, not analytic reality. Carnegie (2025) and Atlantic Council (2025) both call them "durable but diminished."
3. **HTS-victory narrative for Assad's fall.** "HTS defeated Assad in twelve days." Wrong mechanism. The regime fell because four external scaffolds failed simultaneously — Hezbollah, IRGC, Russia/Ukraine, regime army — and HTS walked into a vacuum. The right move is subtraction, not victory.
4. **Conflating primacy, unipolarity, and hegemony.** "The US has been hegemonic in the Middle East since the Cold War." Wrong concept. Gause's (2024) distinction is testable and the US has never had hegemony; conflating the three loses the analytic point of the entire framework.
5. **Treating October 7 as an inexplicable rupture.** "October 7 came out of nowhere." Wrong frame. The Hamas internal documents and Sinwar communications, with caveats, suggest spoiler logic vis-à-vis the imminent Saudi-Israeli normalization track; framing it as inexplicable abandons the strategic-analysis level entirely.
6. **Saying the API "failed."** "The 2002 Arab Peace Initiative failed because Israel rejected it." Wrong verb. The API became the regional template *despite* lack of execution — it was the framework the Abraham Accords *deviated from* and the framework Riyadh has *partially restored* in sequencing terms after October 7. The right move is to treat the API as a sequencing rule rather than a deal, and ask which sequencing rule governs at any given moment.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Final reminder.** Hammad rewards structure and source-citation density. The students who fail this exam aren't the ones who don't know the material — they're the ones who write reactive prose. Outline first, write second.
:::
